title: Harrods Lights Its Facade for Diwali as Luxury Courts Indian Shoppers
excerpt: The Knightsbridge store brings back its Diwali light show for a second year, anchoring a month of Indian designer showcases, gifting and food — and a wider luxury-industry push for the festival.
body:
• Harrods is marking Diwali for a second straight year with a store-wide campaign running through November 8, headlined by a light display across its Knightsbridge facade on November 6, 7 and 8.
  • The programme mixes retail and ritual: a Diwali gift box, an Amrapali trunk show in the store's Penthouse from November 2 to 5, a presenting slot for Indian designer Gaurav Gupta, live music and a saffron milk cake inspired by barfi.
  • Luxury houses are treating Diwali as a serious commercial season, according to WWD, as India's luxury market — valued at about $12 billion by Euromonitor International — ranks among the world's five fastest-growing.
  • The facade light show is free to watch from Brompton Road from 4pm on November 6, 7 and 8. Harrods' ticketed Ranavat saffron skincare masterclass on October 28 costs £25, fully redeemable against products bought on the day.

Harrods will light up its Knightsbridge facade for Diwali for a second consecutive year, turning one of London's most recognisable shopfronts into a canvas of colour for the festival of lights. The display runs for three nights, from November 6 to 8, as the centrepiece of a store-wide Diwali campaign that WWD reports will run through November 8 — a sign that the festival now sits in the store's long-term calendar rather than on its list of one-off promotions.

Three Nights of Light on Brompton Road

The light show, which Harrods debuted in 2025, sends what the store describes as captivating waves of colour cascading across the facade from 4pm each evening. Inside, the campaign runs for weeks rather than days. Harrods' own Diwali at Harrods programme lists a gift box built around cocoa-dusted almonds, turmeric powder and gold coins; a Diwali Saffron Milk Cake at the Food Halls patisserie, inspired by traditional barfi and made with saffron-soaked sponge, whipped Chantilly cream and Dulcey pearls; tea tastings and food sampling from Viras and Laderach; live flautists; and Diwali-inspired make-up looks from beauty brands.

Calligrapher Sai Banerjee will personalise Harrods Collection candles on the Lower Ground Floor across the three light-show days, and the Indian-founded beauty brand Ranavat hosts a ticketed "Saffron Skin Hour" masterclass on October 28. WWD adds the fashion layer: an Amrapali trunk show in the Harrods Penthouse from November 2 to 5, following the UK-India Creative Circle's October 30 party at the Royal Automobile Club with a couture show by Anamika Khanna, and a presentation by Indian designer Gaurav Gupta as part of the Harrods celebration. Across town, Selfridges is hosting Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla at its 40 Duke members' club on October 24 and a Diwali soiree by Rahul Mishra on November 3.

Why Luxury Is Courting Diwali

The commercial logic is spelled out in WWD's reporting. Diwali's five days, from Dhanteras to Bhai Dooj, are built around gifting and buying new things, and this year's main day, Lakshmi Puja, falls on November 8. India's luxury market is valued at approximately $12 billion, according to Euromonitor International, making it one of the five fastest-growing in the world. Brands that have long built campaigns around Lunar New Year and Ramadan are now doing the same maths for Diwali — in India, where Chanel held a Diwali party in Delhi this month with its first Indian ambassador, Ananya Panday, and in diaspora capitals, where Sabyasachi's October 21 reception at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art was the museum's first Diwali event and Cartier again hosted its annual celebration at its Fifth Avenue mansion.

"I don't know that brands have fully grasped how to celebrate Diwali and do it in an authentic way."

— Jessel Taank, publicist for Oushq, quoted by WWD

The Authenticity Test

The same reporting carries a warning. London's Diwali calendar is quieter than last year's, Dubai's is muted despite its large wealthy Indian population, and consultants say brands are judged on whether Diwali appears in their long-term plans and budgets, not on a single season's window dressing. Chhavi Seth Mediratta, who has worked with brands including Tiffany & Co., told WWD that consistency year on year is what engages the diaspora, and that brands should work with South Asian creatives and communities beyond the celebration itself. Harrods, returning for a second year with a bigger in-store programme, is the clearest London example of a retailer passing that test.

What to Watch

For London's Indian community, the practical draw is simple: a flagship, free, public celebration on Brompton Road across November 6 to 8, wrapped around a month of food, beauty and jewellery programming aimed squarely at them. The wider question for the luxury industry is whether next year brings more houses into line behind Harrods — or whether Diwali remains, as WWD's experts put it, a festival still driven more by individuals than by brands.
